# PREFACE.

---

Many have labored to explain the <term>Apocalypse<note>The Book of Revelation, the final book of the Bible, known for its complex and prophetic imagery.</note></term>; however, because the <term>spiritual sense<note>The deeper, symbolic meaning that the author believes lies beneath the literal stories of the Bible.</note></term> of the <term>Word<note>A term used here to refer to the Holy Scriptures or the Bible.</note></term> was previously unknown, they could not perceive the <term>arcana<note>From the Latin word meaning "hidden secrets" or "mysteries."</note></term> stored within it. Only this deeper spiritual understanding can reveal them. Consequently, previous interpreters have relied on guesswork, mostly applying these prophecies to the history of worldly empires and mixing in various church matters. But the Apocalypse, like the entire Word, does not deal with worldly affairs in its spiritual meaning. Instead, it speaks of heavenly things—not of kingdoms and nations, but of heaven and the church.

It should be understood that after the <term>last judgment<note>The author refers to a specific spiritual event he claims to have witnessed in 1757, which he believes reshaped the spiritual world.</note></term>—which took place in the spiritual world in the year 1757 and was described in a separate work published in London in 1758—a New Heaven of Christians was established. This community consists only of those who could accept the truth that the Lord is the God of heaven and earth (according to His words in <note>original: "Matthew xxviii. 18"</note> Matthew 28:18) and who, during their life in the world, had repented of their evil actions.

<summary>This preface introduces the author's claim that the Book of Revelation can only be understood through its "spiritual sense," which relates to heaven and the church rather than political history. It also establishes the historical context of the author's work following a spiritual "last judgment" in 1757.</summary>

<keywords>Apocalypse, Book of Revelation, spiritual sense, Word of God, arcana, last judgment, New Heaven, Swedenborgian theology, repentance</keywords>

That this Church will acknowledge the Lord alone is manifest from these passages in the <term>Apocalypse<note>The Book of Revelation, the final book of the Bible, known for its complex and prophetic imagery.</note></term>: *There came unto me one of the seven angels, and spake with me, saying, "Come, I will show thee the* BRIDE, *the* LAMB’S WIFE": *and he showed me the great City holy Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God* (chapter 21:9, 10). That there is to be a New Heaven, and that a New Church on earth will descend therefrom, is manifest from these words there: *I saw a New Heaven and a New Earth; and I saw the holy City Jerusalem coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a Bride adorned for her Husband. He that sat upon the throne said, "Behold, I make all things new": and He said unto me, "Write, for these words are true and faithful"* (chapter 21:1, 2, 5). 

The New Heaven is a new Heaven formed from Christians; the New Jerusalem is a new Church on earth, which will act as one with that new Heaven. The Lamb is the Lord as to His <term>Divine Human<note>The concept that God’s human form is itself divine, making God approachable and understandable to humanity.</note></term>.

# PREFACE

God as existing in <term>three persons<note>The traditional Christian view of the Trinity, which the author argues can mistakenly lead people to think of three separate Gods.</note></term>, yet who at the same time did not hold the idea of three Gods; and this was because the doctrine of a Trinity of Persons has been accepted throughout the entire Christian world. But those who maintained no other concept of the Lord’s <term>Human<note>Refers to Jesus Christ's physical and psychological nature while on Earth.</note></term> than as the nature of any other man, were unable to receive the faith of the <term>New Jerusalem<note>A symbolic name for a new state of the church and humanity, characterized by a direct relationship with God and a new understanding of spiritual truth.</note></term>; which is, that the Lord is the only God, in whom there is a Trinity. For this reason, these individuals were separated and sent away to the outer regions: I was permitted to see these separations and removals after the <term>last judgment<note>The author refers to a spiritual event he claims to have witnessed in 1757, which he believed reordered the spiritual world to allow for a new era of religious understanding.</note></term>. For the whole of Heaven is founded upon a correct idea of God, as is the entire Church on earth, and indeed all religion; since it is through this idea that there is conjunction with the Divine, and through that conjunction come light, wisdom, and eternal happiness.

Everyone can see that the <term>Apocalypse<note>The Book of Revelation, the final book of the Bible, known for its complex and prophetic imagery.</note></term> can by no means be explained except by the Lord alone; for every word within it contains <term>arcana<note>From the Latin word for 'secrets'; refers to deep, hidden spiritual meanings within the text that are not apparent on the surface.</note></term>, which could never be known without a specific enlightenment, and thus a revelation: for this reason, it has pleased the Lord to open the sight of my spirit and to teach me. Do not believe, therefore, that I have taken anything in this work from myself, nor from any angel, but from the Lord alone. The Lord also said to John through the angel, *“Seal not the words of the prophecy of this Book”* (chapter 22:10); by which is meant that these secrets are to be made manifest.

# A SUMMARY

->OF THE<-

## DOCTRINES OF THE ROMAN CATHOLIC CHURCH AND RELIGION.

---

Since *Babylon*, <note>In this context, the author uses "Babylon" as a symbolic name for the Roman Catholic Church, following a tradition of interpreting the Book of Revelation as a critique of church corruption.</note> which is the Roman Catholic Religion, is also treated of in the Apocalypse <note>The biblical Book of Revelation</note>, chapters xvii., xviii., xix., its doctrinal tenets must first be presented, and in this order: Of Baptism, the Eucharist or Holy Supper, Masses, Repentance, Justification, Purgatory, the Seven Sacraments, the Saints, and Power.

I. Of BAPTISM they teach these things: That Adam, after the offense of disobedience, was wholly changed for the worse as to body and soul: that sin was passed down <note>original: "transfused"</note> into all the human race: that this original sin is taken away only by the merit of Christ; and that the merit of Christ is applied by the Sacrament of Baptism; and that the whole guilt of original sin is thus taken away by Baptism: that in baptized persons there still remains lust <term>theologians often use the term "concupiscence" to describe this lingering inclination toward sin</term> as an incentive to sins, but not sin itself: that they thus put on Christ, become a new creature, and obtain the full and entire remission of their sins. Baptism is called the washing of regeneration <note>original: "regenerationis," meaning rebirth or being made new</note> and of faith. That the baptized, when grown up, are to be questioned concerning the promises made by their sponsors <note>The godparents who spoke for them at their infant baptism</note>, which is the *Sacrament of Confirmation*. That, on account of lapses after Baptism, the Sacrament of Repentance <term>historically referred to as the Sacrament of Penance</term> is necessary.

<summary>This page introduces a systematic summary of Roman Catholic doctrines, beginning with an explanation of Baptism as the means of removing the guilt of original sin inherited from Adam.</summary>
<keywords>Roman Catholicism, Baptism, Original Sin, Adam, Sacrament of Confirmation, Repentance, Babylon, Apocalypse</keywords>

### THE ROMAN CATHOLIC CHURCH.

II. **THE EUCHARIST OR HOLY SUPPER.** That, immediately after consecration, the true body and the true blood of Jesus Christ, together with His Soul and Divinity, are really and substantially contained in the form <note>In this theological context, "form" (or species) refers to the outward appearance of the bread and wine that remains after the substance has changed.</note> of the Bread and Wine—His Body in the form of the Bread, and His Blood in the form of the Wine—by virtue of the words spoken. Yet, the body itself is also contained in the form of the Wine, and the Blood in the form of the Bread, and the Soul in both, by virtue of the natural connection and <term>concomitance</term> <note>The doctrine that because Christ is living and undivided, his Body and Blood cannot be separated; where one is present, the other must be also.</note> by which the parts of the Lord Christ are connected with each other; and the Divinity by reason of its admirable <term>hypostatic union</term> <note>The union of Christ's divine and human natures in one single person.</note> with the body and the soul. Thus, they are just as much contained in either form as in both; in a word, the whole and entire Christ exists in the form of the Bread and in every part of that form, and the whole also in the form of the Wine and in its parts. On this account, the two forms are separated: the Bread is given to the laity, while the Wine is reserved for the clergy. Water is to be mixed with the wine in the cup. The laity shall receive the communion from the clergy, and the clergy shall receive it from themselves. The true Body and true Blood of Christ are in the host after consecration and in the consecrated particles; for that reason, the host is to be adored when it is shown and carried around. This wonderful and singular conversion of the whole substance of the Bread into the Body and the whole substance of the Wine into the Blood is called <term>Transubstantiation</term>. Communion under both forms (both bread and wine) may be granted by the Pope under certain conditions. It is called "supersubstantial Bread" <note>original: "panis supersubstantialis." A term used in some Latin versions of the Lord's Prayer, suggesting bread that is above all essence or provides for the soul.</note> and the "Bread of Angels," which the angels eat without veilings; it is also called spiritual food, and the antidote by which the faithful are delivered from their sins.

III. **MASSES.** It is called the sacrifice of the Mass, since the sacrifice by which Christ offered Himself to God the Father is represented in this under the form of the Bread...

### THE ROMAN CATHOLIC CHURCH.

and Wine; that because of this, there exists in it a sacrifice that is truly <term>propitiatory</term> <note>A sacrifice intended to appease God and atone for sins.</note>, pure, and entirely holy. Furthermore, if the people do not receive communion sacramentally <note>That is, by physically eating the bread and drinking the wine.</note>, but only the minister does so, then the people are said to commune spiritually; this is because the ministers perform the rite not for themselves alone, but for all the faithful who belong to the body of Christ. Masses are not to be performed in the vulgar tongue <note>The "vulgar tongue" refers to the common language spoken by the people, such as Italian, French, or German, as opposed to Latin.</note>, because they contain the great learning of the faithful people; however, the ministers should explain some part of the service on the Lord's days. It is also ordained that certain parts which are mystical should be pronounced in a subdued voice, and others with a louder voice; and in order to provide majesty to such a great sacrifice offered to God, there should be lights, incense, special garments, and other similar items. The Mass is to be offered for the sins, penalties, satisfactions, and various needs of the living, as well as for the dead. Finally, masses held in honor of the saints are acts of thanksgiving for their intercession when they are called upon in prayer.

**IV. REPENTANCE.** <note>Today commonly called the Sacrament of Penance or Reconciliation.</note> That besides Baptism, there is the sacrament of *Repentance*, through which the benefit of Christ's death and merit is applied to those who fall into sin after Baptism; for this reason, it is called a kind of "laborious baptism." The components of *Repentance* are *Contrition*, *Confession*, and *Satisfaction*. *Contrition* is the gift of God and the impulse of the Holy Spirit—not yet living within the person, but merely moving them—and is thus a way of preparing oneself. There must be a *Confession* of all mortal sins, even the most secret, and of the person's intentions; sins that are withheld are not forgiven, but those that do not come to mind after a careful examination are considered included in the confession. Confession should be made at least once a year. Sins are to be absolved by the "ministers of the keys" <note>A reference to the "power of the keys" (Matthew 16:19) believed to be held by the priesthood to forgive or retain sins.</note>; and they are remitted when the priest says, *I absolve* <note>original: "Ego te absolvo"</note>. This *Absolution* is like the act of a judge when a sentence is pronounced. The more grave sins are to be absolved by the bishops, and the most serious of all by the pope. *Satisfaction* is the means by which it is made—

**V. JUSTIFICATION.** That the transmission from that state in which man is born a son of Adam into a state of grace through the second Adam <note>A theological title for Jesus Christ, who restores what was lost by Adam.</note>, the Savior, is not effected without the washing of regeneration <note>A biblical term for the sacrament of Baptism (Titus 3:5).</note> and of faith, or Baptism. That the second beginning of justification is from <term>preventing grace</term> <note>Also known as "prevenient grace," this is the divine influence that precedes any human action, calling the individual to God.</note>, which is a Calling; with which man co-operates by converting himself. That a disposing <note>The process of preparing the soul to receive the grace of being made righteous.</note> is effected by *Faith*, when one believes the things to be true which are revealed, to which he is moved freely; also by *Hope*, while he believes that God is propitious <note>Gracious or merciful.</note> for Christ's sake; and by *Charity* <note>In this context, 'Charity' refers to the theological virtue of supernatural love for God and neighbor.</note>, by which he begins to love the neighbor, and to hate sin. That Justification, which follows, is not only the remission of sins, but sanctification, and the renovation of the inner man: that they are then not reputed just <note>The text emphasizes that the person is not merely "accounted" as righteous in a legal sense (imputation), but is actually made righteous within.</note>, but that they are just, receiving justice into themselves: and that, because they receive the merit of Christ's passion, justification is thus ingrafted by Faith, Hope, and Charity. That Faith is the beginning of human salvation, the foundation and root of Justification; and that this is being justified by faith: and because nothing of those things which precede Justification, whether faith or works, merits the grace of justification, that this is being justified gratuitously <note>Freely given by God's grace, not earned by human effort.</note>, for it is a preventing grace. and that still man is justified by works, and not by faith alone: that the just may fall into light and <term>venial sins</term> <note>Lesser sins that do not break one's relationship with God, as opposed to mortal sins.</note>, and still be just: and that the just ought on that account continually to labor by prayers, oblations, alms, and fasts, lest they fall; because they are born again into the hope of glory, and not into glory <note>Meaning the believer is on the path to heaven but has not yet reached the final state of perfection.</note>. That the Just, if they fall away from the grace of justification, may again be justified by

### THE ROMAN CATHOLIC CHURCH.

...the sacrament of Repentance <note>Commonly known as the Sacrament of Penance or Reconciliation.</note>: that by any <term>mortal sin</term> <note>A grave offense against God's law that destroys the "sanctifying grace" within a person.</note> grace is lost, but not faith; yet that by unbelief, which is a receding from religion, faith also is lost. That the works of the justified man are merits <note>Actions performed by a person in a state of grace that are believed to deserve a reward from God.</note>; and that the justified merit eternal life by those that are done by them through the grace of God and the merit of Christ. That *Free-will* was not lost and extinguished after the sin of Adam; and that man co-operates by assenting to the calling of God; and that otherwise he would be an inanimate body. *Pre-destination* they establish; saying that no one knows whether he is in the number of the predestinated, and among those whom God had elected to Himself, except by special revelation.

**VI. PURGATORY.** That the guilt for which <term>temporal punishment</term> <note>Punishment that must be satisfied either in this life or in Purgatory, distinct from the "eternal punishment" of Hell.</note> is to be suffered is not all blotted out by Justification: that therefore all come into Purgatory, that they may be absolved, before the way is open into heaven. That the souls there detained are helped by the <term>suffrages of the faithful</term> <note>Prayers, intercessions, and pious acts performed by the living for the benefit of the dead.</note>, and especially by the sacrifice of the Mass; and that this is diligently to be taught and preached. The torments there are variously described; but they are inventions, — in themselves figments.

**VII. THE SEVEN SACRAMENTS.** That there are seven sacraments, Baptism, Confirmation, the Eucharist, Repentance, <term>Extreme Unction</term> <note>The anointing of the sick with oil; often called the "Last Rites" when performed near death.</note>, Order <note>Holy Orders, or the ordination of clergy.</note>, and Matrimony: that there are not more, nor less: that one is of greater dignity than another: that they contain grace; and that owing to the <term>work wrought</term> <note>original: "ex opere operato." This doctrine holds that the sacraments are effective by the very fact of the action being performed, independent of the merit of the priest or the recipient.</note> by them grace is conferred: that there were just so many sacraments of the Ancient Law <note>The religious laws and rites of the Old Testament.</note>. Baptism, Confirmation, the Eucharist, and Repentance, have been treated of above. The *Sacrament of Extreme Unction*: that it is from James v. 14, 15: that it is done to the sick near the end of life; whence it is called the sacrament of the departing: that if they recover, it may be applied again: that it is done with oil blessed by a bishop, and in these words: "May God grant thee indulgence for whatever <note>The text breaks off here; this is the beginning of the traditional Latin formula for the anointing.</note>

<meta>This page continues the summary of Roman Catholic doctrine, moving from the sacraments of Penance and Purgatory into the specific rituals of anointing, the structure of the priesthood, the rules of marriage, and the role of saints and religious imagery.</meta>

### THE ROMAN CATHOLIC CHURCH.

...[that through this holy anointing, the Lord forgives] whatever sins you have committed through fault of the eyes, of the nostrils, or of the touch." <note>This is the conclusion of the section on the Sacrament of Extreme Unction, now known as the Anointing of the Sick. During the ritual, a priest would anoint the various sense organs of the dying person while reciting this formula.</note> **The Sacrament of Holy Orders**: that there are seven levels in the Ministry of the Priesthood, which differ in rank, and together are called the <term>Ecclesiastical Hierarchy</term> <note>The structured ranking of church officials, from the lower orders up to the Pope.</note>, which is like the orderly arrangement of a military camp. They believe that initiations into this ministry are performed through anointings and by the passing of the Holy Spirit into the ministers. Furthermore, the ordination of Bishops and Priests does not require the authority of secular governments, nor the consent or calling of civil magistrates. Those who are appointed only by civil authority and "climb up" to the ministry are not true ministers, but "thieves and robbers" <note>A biblical reference to John 10:1, suggesting that those who do not enter the ministry through the proper church channels are illegitimate.</note> who do not enter through the proper door. **The Sacrament of Matrimony**: that the power to grant dispensations for marriage and to decide on divorces belongs to the Church. They hold that the clergy shall not marry; that they can all receive the gift of <term>chastity</term> <note>The state of refraining from sexual relations, specifically in a religious context.</note>, and if anyone says he cannot remain chaste even after taking a vow, let him be <term>anathema</term> <note>Formally cursed or excommunicated by the church.</note>. This is because God does not deny this gift to those who seek it rightly, and does not allow anyone to be tempted beyond what they can endure. Finally, the state of virginity and celibacy is to be preferred over the married state, among other regulations.

**VIII. THE SAINTS.** They believe that the Saints, who reign together with Christ, offer their <term>orisons</term> <note>An older word for prayers.</note> to God on behalf of humanity. While Christ is to be adored, the saints are to be invoked (called upon for help). They argue that the invocation of saints is not idolatry, nor does it take away from the honor of the one Mediator between God and men. This highest form of worship is called <term>Divine Adoration</term> <note>original: *latria*; a theological term for the supreme worship offered to God alone, as opposed to the honor given to saints.</note>. They also maintain that images of Christ, of Mary the mother of God, and of the saints, are to be respected and honored. This is not because they believe divinity or power exists within the physical objects themselves, but because the honor shown to the image is directed toward the <term>prototypes</term> <note>The original person or holy figure that the statue or painting represents.</note> which they represent. Through these images—which the faithful kiss, and before which they kneel and uncover their heads—they adore Christ and honor the saints. Finally, they believe that God performs miracles through the influence of the saints.

### THE ROMAN CATHOLIC CHURCH.

**IX. POWER.** That the Pope of Rome is the successor of the apostle Peter, and the <term>vicar</term> <note>From the Latin *vicarius*, meaning a representative or deputy who acts in the place of another; here, the earthly representative of Christ.</note> of Jesus Christ, — the head of the Church, and the universal bishop: that he is above Councils: that he has the keys to open and shut heaven <note>A reference to the "Keys of the Kingdom" mentioned in the Gospel of Matthew (16:19), symbolizing the authority to grant or deny entrance into heaven.</note>, and thus the power of remitting and retaining sins: that to him, therefore, as the key-bearer of eternal life, the rights at once of earthly and heavenly empire belong: that from him also the bishops and priests have such power, because it was also given to the rest of the apostles; and that on that account they are called ministers of the keys. That it is for the Church to judge of the true sense and interpretation of the Sacred Scripture; and that they who oppose it are to be punished by penalties established by law. That it is not fitting for the <term>laity</term> <note>Ordinary people who are members of the church but are not ordained as clergy.</note> to read the Sacred Scripture, since no one knows the sense of it but the Church: hence her ministers make traffic of their knowledge of it.

**X.** The above are from Councils and <term>Bulls</term> <note>An official decree or public announcement issued by a Pope, named after the *bulla* or lead seal used to authenticate the document.</note>, especially from the Council of Trent <note>A major ecumenical council of the Roman Catholic Church held between 1545 and 1563, which defined church doctrine in response to the Protestant Reformation.</note> and the papal Bull confirming it; wherein they condemn by <term>anathema</term> <note>A formal curse or excommunication by the Church, cutting a person off from the community of believers.</note> all who think, believe, and do contrary to the things which were decreed, which in general are adduced above.

### III. OF JUSTIFICATION BY FAITH, AND OF GOOD WORKS.

The justifying and saving faith of the clergy is this: that God the Father turned Himself away from the human race on account of their iniquities <note>Sins or gross injustices.</note>, and so from justice condemned them to eternal death; and that on that account He sent the Son into the world, to expiate <note>To make amends or pay the penalty for a wrongdoing.</note> and redeem, and to satisfy and to reconcile; and that the Son did this by His taking upon Himself the condemnation of the Law, and suffering Himself to be crucified; and that in this manner and by obedience He fulfilled all God’s justice, so far that He became justice; and that this justice as His merit God the Father imputes <note>To "impute" is a legal or accounting term meaning to credit something to someone else's account—in this case, crediting Christ's righteousness to the believer.</note> and applies to believers; and sends to them the Holy Spirit, who operates charity, good works, and repentance, as a good tree bears good fruit; and justifies, renews, regenerates, and sanctifies them: and that this faith is the only means of salvation; and that by it alone sins are remitted <note>Forgiven or canceled.</note> to man. They distinguish between the act and the state of Justification. By the act of justification they mean the commencement of justification; which takes place at the moment when a man, by that faith alone, takes hold of the merit of Christ with confidence. By the state of Justification they mean the progress of that faith, which is effected by the interior operation of the Holy Spirit; which does not manifest itself except by certain signs, about which they teach various things. They teach also manifest good works, which are done by the man and his will, and which follow that faith; but they exclude them from justifi- <note>The text breaks off here; it likely concludes with "justification."</note>

They maintain, besides, that at the last judgment Christ is to pass sentence upon good and evil works, as the effects, proper and not proper to man's faith. This faith reigns at this day among the clergy in the whole Reformed Church.

<meta>This page continues the technical description of Reformed and Lutheran doctrines. While the previous page focused on the mechanics of how the Holy Spirit initiates conversion, this page shifts to how these complex doctrines are understood—or misunderstood—by ordinary people compared to the professional clergy.</meta>

<page-num>21</page-num>
<header>THE REFORMED CHURCH.</header>

This theological system is accepted across the Reformed Christian world; however, it is not truly held by the laity <note>Ordinary church members who are not members of the clergy</note>, except for a very few. For the laity understand "faith" to mean nothing more than believing in God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and the idea that whoever lives a good life and holds a right belief will be saved—and that the Lord is the Saviour. They are generally unaware of the complex "mysteries of <term>justification</term>" <note>The specific theological process of how a person is made right with God</note> preached by their ministers. Even when these ministers preach such things, the concepts tend to go in one ear and out the other for the average listener.

Nevertheless, the teachers consider themselves highly learned for knowing these details and spend a great deal of effort in their colleges and universities to master them. For this reason, it was stated earlier that this specific form of faith is primarily the "faith of the clergy." Even so, the teachers present this same faith in different ways depending on the kingdom:

In *Germany, Sweden*, and *Denmark*: They teach that the Holy Spirit works through this faith to <term>justify</term> and <term>sanctify</term> <note>To make a person holy or set them apart for God</note> people. Afterward, it gradually renews and regenerates them, but without including the "works of the Law" <note>The idea that following the Ten Commandments or religious rules contributes to salvation</note>. They believe that those who hold this faith with total trust are in God the Father’s grace, and while the sins they commit are still visible, those sins are constantly being forgiven.

In *England*: They teach that this faith produces <term>charity</term> <note>In this context, charity refers to active love and good works toward one's neighbor</note> without the person even being aware of it. They also suggest that a person might feel the Holy Spirit working within them. If a person does not feel this inner movement but still does good deeds for the sake of being saved, those deeds might be called "good," but they are still considered to have "merit" <note>The controversial idea that a human can earn or take credit for their own salvation</note> coming from the person rather than God. They also suggest this faith can work its effects at the very hour of death, though the exact method is unknown.

In *Holland*: They teach that God the Father, for the sake of the Son and through the Holy Spirit, justifies and purifies a person’s inner self through faith. However, they believe this process steers clear of the person's own will <note>Their choices and desires</note>, which God turns away from without touching. Some teach that He touches the will only lightly, so that the evils present in a person’s will do not appear in the sight of God. 

Very few of the common people are familiar with these theological "mysteries." Furthermore, the clergy are often unwilling to publish these doctrines exactly as they are, because they know that the general public would not find them agreeable.

<summary>This page explores the disconnect between complex clerical doctrines on justification and the simpler faith of the laity, noting regional differences in how Reformed theology is taught in Germany, England, and Holland.</summary>

### **IV. THE LAW AND THE GOSPEL.**

God gave the Law so that we might recognize what sin is. Its purpose is to restrain sin through threats and fear, while also leading us toward the promise and announcement of God’s grace. Therefore, the primary job of the Law is to reveal <term>original sin</term> <note>The theological concept that human nature is inherently inclined toward selfishness and evil as a result of the Fall</note> and all its various fruits. It shows us the horrible extent to which human nature has fallen and how deeply it has been corrupted. 

By this means, the Law terrifies, humbles, and prostrates a person until they lose all hope in their own power and anxiously desire help. This effect of the Law is called <term>Contrition</term> <note>A deep, painful realization of one's own spiritual failings</note>. This is not "active" (something a person does) or "factitious" (manufactured), but is "passive"—it is the actual torture of a person’s conscience. 

The Gospel, however, is the complete doctrine regarding Christ and faith, and thus regarding the <term>remission of sins</term> <note>The forgiveness or "sending away" of sins</note>. Consequently, it is the most joyful messenger; it does not accuse or terrify, but comforts. Through the Law, God’s anger against all wickedness is revealed and man is condemned; for this reason, the Law causes a person to look toward Christ and the Gospel. Both the Law and the Gospel must be preached, because they are joined together. 

The Gospel teaches that Christ took the entire "curse of the Law" upon Himself and <term>expiated</term> <note>Paid the penalty for or cleansed</note> all sins, and that we obtain forgiveness through faith. It teaches that the Holy Spirit is given and received—and the heart of man is renewed—through the preaching of the Gospel, not the Law. 

The Spirit then uses the "ministry of the Law" to teach and point out, through the <term>Decalogue</term> <note>The Ten Commandments</note>, what God’s good will and pleasure actually are. In this manner, the Spirit "makes dead" (the old self) and "makes alive" (the new self). A distinction must be made between the "works of the Law" and the "works of the Spirit." Because of this, believers—insofar as they are believers—are not "under the Law," but "under grace." 

The righteousness of the Law does not <term>justify</term> <note>The process of being declared righteous or "made right" before God</note> a person; that is, it does not reconcile them to God, nor regenerate them, nor make them acceptable to God on its own. However, when the Holy Spirit is given, the fulfilling of the Law follows naturally. The works of the <term>second table</term> <note>The section of the Ten Commandments dealing with duties toward other people, such as "thou shalt not kill" or "thou shalt not steal"</note> of the Decalogue do not justify us, because through them we are dealing with other people, rather than properly dealing with God.

<summary>This page outlines the relationship between the Law and the Gospel in Reformed theology, explaining how the Law reveals human corruption and causes contrition, while the Gospel provides comfort and the Holy Spirit. It emphasizes that while the Law cannot save a person, it serves as a guide for those who have been renewed by faith.</summary>
<keywords>Law and Gospel, Contrition, Decalogue, Original Sin, Justification, Holy Spirit, Ten Commandments, Grace, Second Table of the Law</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the relationship between divine grace and human action, transitioning from the distinction between the Law and the Gospel to the specific practices of repentance, confession, and the foundational problem of original sin.</meta>

<page-num>23</page-num>
<header>THE REFORMED CHURCH.</header>

...and yet in <term>justification</term> <note>The theological process of being declared righteous or "in the right" before God</note> we must act with God. Because Christ was without sin, He suffered the punishment for sin and was made an offering for us; He took away the Law's claim to condemn believers. He serves as a <term>propitiation</term> <note>A sacrifice that restores a broken relationship by removing guilt</note> for them, and for His sake, they are regarded as just.

### V. REPENTANCE AND CONFESSION

Repentance consists of two parts: one is <term>Contrition</term> <note>A deep sense of guilt and sorrow for one's sins</note>, which is the terror felt in the conscience because of sin; the other is faith, which is born from the Gospel. This faith comforts the conscience by the <term>remission of sins</term> <note>The formal forgiveness or "sending away" of sins</note> and frees it from those terrors. A person who confesses that they are entirely made of sin includes all their sins, excludes none, and forgets none: in this way, the sins are cleared away and the person is purified, set right, and made holy, since the Holy Spirit does not allow sin to rule but instead holds it back and restrains it. 

The listing of specific sins during confession should be done freely, as the person chooses; however, private confession and <term>absolution</term> <note>The formal declaration by a minister that a person's sins are forgiven</note> are to be held in high regard. Therefore, if someone wishes, they may confess their sins and receive absolution from a Confessor, and the sins are then forgiven. The words the Minister uses to respond are:

-> “May God be <term>propitious</term> <note>original: "propitius" — meaning mercifully inclined or favorable</note> to you and strengthen your faith; may it be done for you as you believe; and by the Lord’s command, I forgive your sins.” <-

But others use this phrasing:

-> “I announce to you the forgiveness of your sins.” <-

Yet, it is held that sins are not forgiven because of the act of repentance or by good works, but through faith alone. Therefore, repentance as practiced by the clergy is simply a confession before God that they are sinners and a petition that they may remain steady in their faith. Acts of <term>expiation</term> <note>The act of making amends or paying a penalty for a crime</note> and <term>satisfaction</term> <note>Specific tasks or prayers performed to show penance</note> are not necessary, because Christ is the ultimate expiation and satisfaction.

### VI. OF ORIGINAL SIN.

They teach that since the fall of Adam, all human beings born through natural birth are born with sin—that is, without the fear of God and with <term>concupiscences</term> <note>Disordered desires or a natural inclination toward selfish and sinful urges</note>. This condition brings condemnation and eternal death to those who are not born again through Baptism and by

That this evil is covered over and pardoned by Christ alone: that the seed itself from which a man is formed is contaminated by that sin: that it is hence also, that a man receives from his parents depraved inclinations and internal uncleanness of heart.

### VII. BAPTISM.

That **Baptism** is not simply water, but that it is water taken by the Divine command, and sealed by the Word of God, and thus made holy: that the virtue, work, fruit, and end of Baptism is, that men should be saved, and be <term>elected</term> <note>Formally chosen or brought into the community of believers.</note> into the Christian communion: that through Baptism there is proffered victory over death and the devil, remission of sins, the grace of God, Christ with all His works, and the Holy Spirit with all His gifts, and eternal blessedness to all and each that believe: whether faith also is given to infants by Baptism, is a thing too high to be urgently inquired into. That immersion into the water signifies the <term>mortification</term> <note>The spiritual "killing off" or suppression of sinful desires and the old way of life.</note> of the old

But others of the Reformed believe that Baptism is an external washing with water, by which internal <term>ablution</term> <note>A formal act of washing or cleansing, here referring to the cleansing of the soul from sin.</note> from sins is signified : that it does not confer regeneration, faith, the grace of God, and salvation, but only signifies and seals them ; and that they are not conferred in and with Baptism, but afterwards with increasing age ; and that only the **elect** <note>Those whom God has chosen for salvation, according to specific theological traditions.</note> obtain the grace of Christ and the gift of faith : and because salvation does not depend on Baptism, that in the lack of a regular minister it is therefore permitted to be done by another person.

### VIII. **THE HOLY SUPPER.**

The Reformed who are called Lutherans <note>In the early Reformation era, the term "Reformed" was often used broadly for all Protestant groups. Here, the author uses it to categorize those who followed Martin Luther's specific teachings as a subset of the broader movement.</note> teach, that in the **Holy Supper** or **Sacrament of the Altar**, the Body and Blood of Christ are truly and **substantially** present ; and that they are truly distributed and received together with the Bread and the Wine ; and that on that account the true Body and true Blood of Christ are in, with, and under the Bread and Wine, and are given to Christians to eat and drink : and that for that reason they are not simply bread and wine, but are included in and bound to the Word of God ; and that this causes them to be the Body and Blood of Christ : for when the Word is added to the elements, they become a Sacrament : yet that it is not **transubstantiation** <note>The Roman Catholic doctrine that the bread and wine physically change into the substance of Christ's body and blood, leaving only the appearance of bread and wine.</note>, such as the papists claim : that it is the food of the soul, nourishing and strengthening the new man : that it was instituted,

IX. **FREE-WILL.** They distinguish between the state before the fall, after the fall, after the reception of faith and renovation <note>The process of being spiritually made new or "born again."</note>, and after the resurrection. That man, since the fall, can begin, think, understand, believe, will, operate, and co-operate absolutely nothing in spiritual and Divine things from his own powers; nor apply or accommodate himself to grace; but that his natural will is only unto those things which are contrary to God, and displeasing to God: consequently that man in spiritual things is like a **stock** <term>original: "truncus"; a theological metaphor comparing a person's spiritual state to a lifeless tree trunk or log, incapable of movement without outside help.</term>; but that he still has capacity, not active but passive, by which he may by the grace of God be turned to good: yet that the free-will left to man since the fall is, to be able and not to be able to hear the Word of God; and that thus a little spark of faith is enkindled in his heart, which embraces the remission of sins for Christ’s sake, and gives comfort. Yet that the human will has liberty as to the doing of **civil justice** <term>original: "iustitia civilis"; refers to outward moral behavior and following the laws of society, which even a non-believer can achieve through reason.</term> and the choice of matters subject to reason.

X. **THE CHURCH.** That the Church is the congregation and communion of the saints; and that it is spread through the entire world with those who have the same Christ and the same Holy Spirit, and the same Sacraments; whether they have similar or dissimilar traditions: and that it is principally a society of faith: and that this Church alone is the body of Christ; and that the good are the Church in reality and in name, but the evil only in name. That the evil and hypocrites, because they are intermixed, are members of the Church according to its external signs, provided they are not excommunicated; but that they are not members of Christ’s body. That the ecclesiastical rites, which are called ceremonies, are **indifferent** <term>original: "adiaphora"; actions or rituals that are not specifically commanded or forbidden by Scripture and are therefore considered optional.</term>; and that they are not the worship of God,

### THE EXPLANATION.

1. What the spiritual sense is has been hitherto unknown. That it is in every thing in <term>the Word; a term used here to refer to the Sacred Scriptures or the Bible.</term>, and that the Word in many places cannot be understood without it, has been shown in the "*Doctrine of the New Jerusalem concerning the Sacred Scripture*," n. 5-26. That sense does not appear in the sense of the letter; for it is within it, as the soul is in the body. It is known that there is the spiritual and the natural; and that the spiritual flows in into the natural, and presents itself to be seen and felt in the forms which fall under the sight and the touch; and that without them the spiritual is not otherwise perceived than as affection and thought, or as love and wisdom, which are of the mind. It is acknowledged that affection

Hence it is manifest, that there is a perfect union of spiritual things and natural things in man. It is similar in each and every thing in the world. There is there the spiritual, which is the inmost of the cause; and there is the natural, which is its effect; and the two make one: and in the natural the spiritual does not appear; because the latter is within the former as the soul is in the body, and as the inmost of the cause is in the effect, as was said. It is similar with <term>the Word; the author’s term for the Sacred Scriptures or Bible, which he believes contains hidden layers of meaning.</term>: that this interiorly is spiritual, because it is Divine, can be denied by no one. But as the spiritual does not appear in the sense of the letter, which is natural, the spiritual sense has for that reason been hitherto unknown: nor could it be made known until genuine truths were revealed by the Lord, for that sense is in these. This is the reason that the <term>Apocalypse; from the Greek 'apokalypsis', meaning an uncovering or 'revelation' of hidden things.</term> has not hitherto been understood. But lest there should be doubt that such things are within it, they are to be explained one by one, and to be demonstrated by similar things elsewhere in the Word. The explanation and demonstration now follow.

### 6. *Who testified the Word of God, and the testimony of Jesus Christ*

This signifies those who receive <term>Divine truth <gloss>The spiritual light and wisdom that flows from God into the human mind.</gloss></term> from the Word from the heart and thus in the light, and who acknowledge that the **Lord’s Human is Divine**. It is said of John that he testified the Word of God; but since all who are in the **good of life** <note>The "good of life" refers to living according to one's religious beliefs through practical, kind actions.</note> from charity and its faith are meant by **John** (as was stated just above in section 5), therefore in the <term>spiritual sense <gloss>The deeper, symbolic meaning of the Bible that relates to the soul and heaven, rather than just historical events.</gloss></term> all those people are meant. 

The **angels**, who perceive the spiritual sense of the Word, do not know any specific names of persons mentioned in the Word. Instead, they only recognize what that person represents and signifies. For **John**, this representation is the **good of life**, or "good in act"; consequently, he represents the collective body of everyone who lives in that good. These people "testify"—that is, they see, acknowledge, and receive truth from the heart in spiritual light, and they confess the truths of the Word. They especially acknowledge the central truth that the **Lord’s Human is Divine**, as evidenced by the many scriptural passages cited in the *Doctrine of the New Jerusalem concerning the Lord* <note>One of Swedenborg's primary works, which argues that Jesus Christ is the one God of heaven and earth, holding a fully Divine humanity.</note>. 

By **Jesus Christ** and by the **Lamb** in the **Apocalypse** <note>The Book of Revelation.</note> is meant the Lord in His <term>Divine Human <gloss>The state of the Lord after the resurrection, where His human nature became fully one with His Divine essence.</gloss></term>, and by **God** is meant the Lord as the Divine essence itself from which all things originate. 

As for the spiritual meaning of **testifying**, it is used in relation to **Truth** because in this world, truth must be proven or "attested" before it is accepted. However, in heaven, truth testifies to itself because it is the very **light of heaven**. When angels hear the truth, they immediately recognize it within themselves and acknowledge it. Because the Lord is the truth itself (as He teaches in John 14:6), in heaven He is His own testimony. This clarifies what is meant by "the testimony of Jesus Christ." For this reason, the Lord says: *You sent to John, and he testified to the truth; yet I do not receive testimony from man* (John 5:33). And again: *John came for a witness...*

### 7. *Whatsoever things he saw*

This signifies their **enlightenment** <note>Enlightenment here is not a general intellectualism, but a specific spiritual gift where one perceives the inner truth of the Word.</note> in all the things which are in this **Revelation**. By "whatsoever things he saw" are not meant in the <term>spiritual sense <gloss>The internal, symbolic meaning of scripture that describes the state of heaven and the soul.</gloss></term> the things which **John** saw—these were only visions—but the things which they see who are meant by **John**; who are those that are in **good of life** <note>Living a "good of life" means practicing kindness and integrity based on one's religious convictions.</note> from **charity** and its **faith**; as has been said above. These see in John's visions the <term>arcana <gloss>From the Latin for "hidden things"; deep spiritual secrets or mysteries.</gloss></term> concerning the state of the **Church**; not so much when they read them themselves, but when they see them revealed.

Besides, to **see** signifies to **understand**; for which reason it is also said in common speech, that one "sees" that matter, and that he "sees" that it is the truth: for the spirit of man has sight as well as his body. But by his spirit a man sees **spiritual things**, because from the light of **heaven**; but with his body **natural things**, because from the light of the **world**: and spiritual things are **real**, but natural things are their **forms**. The sight of man's spirit is what is called the **understanding**. It is manifest from this, what is meant in the spiritual sense by "whatsoever things he saw;" and so too in what follows, where it is said that he saw.

In heaven, a person is recognized by their specific office and function. Every man, spirit, and angel there is named according to this; therefore, when a "prophet" is mentioned, because his function was to write and teach the **Word**, it refers to the **Word** itself in its doctrinal form. This is why the **Lord**, as He is the **Word** itself, was also called a **Prophet** (Deut. xviii. 15–20; Matt. xiii. 57; xxi. 11; Luke xiii. 33).

*...shall receive a prophet's reward; and whoever shall receive a righteous man in the name of a righteous man, shall receive a righteous man's reward* (Matthew x. 41). To receive a **prophet** "in the name of a prophet" is to receive the truth of **doctrine** simply because it is true; and to receive a **righteous man** "in the name of a righteous man" is to receive what is **good** for the sake of goodness itself; and to receive a **reward** is to be saved according to how one has received these things. It is clear that no one receives a heavenly reward, or is saved, merely because he welcomes a prophet or a righteous person in a literal, physical sense. Without a deeper knowledge of what a **prophet** and a **righteous man** signify spiritually, these words cannot be understood by anyone; nor can the words that follow: *Whosoever shall give to drink unto one of these little ones a cup of cold water only in the name of a disciple, shall not lose his reward* (Matthew x. 42). It is manifest that a reward is not intended for the literal **prophets** only, and that it is not only the historical **apostles** and **prophets** who are to rejoice when the <term>Last Judgment <gloss>The final resolution of spiritual states at the end of a religious era.</gloss></term> takes place. Instead, all will do so who have received the truths of doctrine and lived according to them: these individuals are therefore what is meant by the **apostles** and **prophets**.

10. **John to the seven churches**, signifies to all who are in the Christian world, where the Word <note>The "Word" refers to the Sacred Scripture or the Bible.</note> is, and by it the Lord is known, and who draw near to the church. By the **Seven Churches** are not meant seven specific churches, but all who belong to the Church throughout the Christian world; for numbers in the Word signify things, and **seven** signifies "all," and therefore also "full" and "perfect." This number is used in the Word where a holy thing is discussed, and in the opposite sense, a profane thing: for this reason, that number involves holiness, and in the opposite sense, profaneness. 

The reason that numbers signify things—or rather, that they act like certain adjectives to substantives, adding a specific quality to the subject—is because number in itself is natural. Natural things are defined by numbers, but spiritual things are defined by their qualities and their states. Therefore, he who does not know the meaning of the numbers in the Word, and especially in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>, cannot know many <term>arcana</term> <note>Latin for "secrets" or "mysteries"; refers here to the hidden spiritual truths contained within the literal sense of the Bible.</note> which are contained therein. Now, since by **seven** all are signified, it is clear that by "the Seven Churches" are meant all who are in the Christian world where the Word is and the Lord is known through it. If these people live according to the Lord’s precepts in the Word, they constitute the Church itself. 

It is for this reason that the **Sabbath** was established on the **seventh day**, and that the **seventh year** was called the sabbatical year, and the **seven times seventh year** the Jubilee; by these was signified everything that is holy in the Church. <page-num>53</page-num>
<header>No. 17.] THE APOCALYPSE REVEALED.</header>

...truth in doctrine and in faith is the first and primary concern of the church—and thus the <term>First-born</term> <note>In the biblical tradition, the first-born son held the right of inheritance and leadership. Here, Swedenborg discusses whether "truth" or "good action" holds that primary status.</note>—shall now be discussed.

They believed this because truth is learned first, and because the church becomes a church by means of it; yet, the church does not truly exist within a person until that truth becomes part of their life. Previously, it exists only in the thought of the understanding and in the memory, not in the act of the will. Truth which is not expressed in act or work does not live: it is like a tree luxuriant in branches and leaves but without fruit; it is like knowledge without application to use, or like the foundation upon which a house is built, which is meant to be lived in. 

These things are the first in terms of *time*, but they are not the first in terms of *purpose* (<term>end</term>); and the things that are first in purpose are the truly primary ones. For the first thing in purpose is to reside in the house, whereas the first in time is the foundation. Likewise, the first thing in purpose is the use, while the first in time is the knowledge. So too, the first thing in purpose when a tree is planted is the fruit, but the first in time are the branches and leaves. 

It is the same with the understanding, which is the first thing formed in a man, but for the purpose that what a man sees with his understanding, he may actually do. Otherwise, the understanding is like a preacher who teaches well but lives wickedly. 

Moreover, every truth is sown in the <term>internal man</term> <note>The "internal man" refers to the inner spiritual mind where intentions and thoughts are formed.</note> and rooted in the <term>external man</term> <note>The "external man" refers to the natural, physical life where one interacts with the world.</note>. For this reason, unless the truth that has been sown is rooted in the external man—which is done through action—it is like a tree set not in the ground, but above it, which withers away immediately when breathed upon by the heat of the sun. This "root" is what the person who has lived the truths carries with them after death; but this is not the case for the person who has only known and acknowledged them through "faith alone." 

Now, because many of the ancients made that which is first in *time* the first in *purpose* (the primary thing), they therefore claimed that the **First-born** signified truth in doctrine and in faith within the church. They did not realize that this is the first-born only in appearance, not in actuality. But all those who made truth in doctrine and in faith the primary concern were condemned, because they included nothing of deed or...

Swedenborg uses analogies of houses and fruit trees to argue that "faith alone" without a life of use is like a foundation without a house or a tree without fruit.</summary>

There are two kingdoms into which the universal heaven is distinguished, the spiritual kingdom and the heavenly (celestial) kingdom. <note>original: *celeste*. Swedenborg divides heaven into two main "kingdoms": the Spiritual, characterized by those who act from a clear understanding of truth, and the Celestial, characterized by those who act directly from a heart full of love.</note> The spiritual kingdom is what is called the Lord’s royalty; and because all who are there are in wisdom from truths, they are therefore meant by the kings which the Lord will make those to be who are in wisdom from Him: and the heavenly kingdom is what is called the Lord’s priesthood; and because all who are there are in love from goods, they are therefore meant by the priests which the Lord will make those to be, who are in love from Him. In like manner is the Lord’s Church on earth distinguished into two kingdoms. ### 21.
*Unto God and His Father*, signifies and thus images of His Divine Wisdom and His Divine Love. By God and the Father in the spiritual sense are not meant two persons; but by God is meant the Divine as to Wisdom, and by the Father the Divine as to Love. For there are two things in the Lord, the Divine Wisdom and the Divine Love, or the Divine Truth and the Divine Good. These two are meant in the Old Testament by God and Jehovah, and here by God and the Father. Now as the Lord teaches that He and the Father are one, and that He is in the Father and the Father in Him (John 10:30; 14:10, 11); by God and the Father two persons are not meant, but the Lord alone. The Divine also is one and indivisible; for which reason by Jesus Christ having made us kings and priests unto God and His Father, is signified that they appear before Him as images of His Divine Wisdom and His Divine Love. In these two things also does the image of God in men and angels consist. ### 22.
*To Him be glory and strength for ever and ever*, signifies Who alone has Divine Majesty and Divine Omnipotence to eternity. By “glory” in the Word <note>The "Word" is the term the author uses for the Holy Scripture or the Bible.</note>, where the Lord is spoken of, the Divine Majesty is meant, and it is predicated of <note>To be "predicated of" means that this quality is specifically associated with a certain aspect; here, Majesty is the outward expression of Wisdom.</note> His Divine Wisdom; and by “strength” is meant the Divine Omnipotence, and it is predicated of His Divine Love; and by “for ever and ever” is meant eternity. ### 23.

Clouds appear in the spiritual world equally as in the natural world. The reason is, that the light of heaven there is the Divine Truth, and darkness there is falsities. church; and by "brethren," he means those who live in charity <term>charity: in Swedenborg's writing, this refers not just to giving alms, but to the active practice of goodwill and justice in one's daily life</term>. Because the good of charity is what constitutes a "brother" in a spiritual sense, the Lord therefore calls those who live accordingly His brethren, as seen in Matthew 25:40, and also addresses the disciples this way (Matthew 28:10; John 20:17). 

However, we do not read that the disciples ever called the Lord "brother," because a "brother" signifies the goodness that comes *from* the Lord. This is similar to how a king, a prince, or a nobleman might call their relatives and neighbors "brothers," yet those individuals do not address the ruler as "brother" in return. For the Lord says: *One is your Teacher, Christ, but all you are brethren* (Matthew 23:8); and also, *You call Me Master and Lord, and you say well, for I am* (John 13:13). 

The sons of Israel called everyone "brethren" who descended from their father Jacob, and in a broader sense, they included those descended from Esau; but those who did not share this lineage were called "companions." But as the Word <note>original: "Verbum"; Swedenborg uses "The Word" to refer specifically to the Sacred Scripture as a vessel for divine truth</note> in its spiritual sense <term>spiritual sense: the deeper, symbolic meaning of the Bible that relates to the human soul and the afterlife, rather than just historical events</term> deals only with those who are in the Lord's Church, "brethren" in that sense means those who are in the good of charity from the Lord, while "companions" refers to those who are in the truths of faith. 

This distinction is found in the following passages: 
*Thus shall you say every one to his companion, and every one to his brother, "What has Jehovah answered?"* (Jeremiah 23:35). 
*You have not proclaimed liberty every one to his brother and every one to his companion* (Jeremiah 34:17). 
*Let no one press his companion nor his brother* (Deuteronomy 15:1, 2). 
*For my brethren and companions' sake I will say* (Psalms 122:8). 
*Every one helps his companion, and says to his brother, "Strengthen yourself"* (Isaiah 41:6). 

The terms are also used in an opposite sense <note>In Swedenborg's system of "correspondences," words can have an "opposite sense" representing the perversion of good and truth into evil and falsehood</note>: 
*Beware for yourselves every one of his companion, and trust not upon any brother: every brother supplants, and every companion is a slanderer* (Jeremiah 9:4). 
*I will mingle Egypt with Egypt, that he may fight against his brother and against his companion* (Isaiah 19:2, and in other places). 

These examples are cited so that it may be understood why John calls himself a "brother and companion"—to show that a "brother" in the Word signifies someone who is in charity or goodness, and a "com-

33. *In affliction, and in the kingdom and the patient expectation of Jesus Christ,* signifies those things which in the church are infested by evils and falsities <term>falsities: specific religious errors or wrongheaded beliefs that lead people away from spiritual truth</term>; but these are to be removed by the Lord, when He comes. By **affliction** is meant the state of the church when there are no longer any goods of charity and truths of faith, but evils and falsities in place of them. By **the kingdom** is meant the church; and by **the patient expectation of Jesus Christ** is meant the Lord’s coming. Therefore, these words—*“In affliction, and in the kingdom and the patient expectation of Jesus Christ”*—when gathered into one single meaning, signify the time when the goods and truths of the church are under attack by evils and falsities, and the promise that these will be removed by the Lord at His coming. 

That "affliction" means the state of the church when it is overrun by evils and falsities is clear from these passages: *In the consummation of the age* <note>original: "consummatione saeculi"; this refers to the end of a particular spiritual era or "church age," rather than the physical destruction of the world</note> *they shall deliver you into affliction, and shall kill you. There shall be great affliction, such as hath not been from the beginning of the world, nor shall be. After the affliction of those days the sun shall be darkened, the moon shall not give her light, and the stars shall fall from heaven* (Matthew 24:9, 21, 29; Mark 13:19, 24). That “the kingdom” signifies the Church will be seen in the sections that follow.

In the spiritual sense, **islands** signify nations that are more remote from the direct worship of God, but which are nevertheless destined to draw near to it because they are capable of being enlightened. 36. ***I became in the spirit on the Lord's day***, signifies a spiritual state at that time arising from Divine influx <term>influx: the spiritual "flowing in" of life, light, and truth from God into the human mind</term>. **I became in the spirit** signifies the spiritual state in which he was while experiencing the visions, a description of which follows. **On the Lord's day** signifies influx at that time from the Lord; for on that day there is a special presence of the Lord, because the day is holy. From this it is evident that "I became in the spirit on the Lord's day" signifies a spiritual state then resulting from Divine influx.

Of the prophets we read that they were "in the spirit" or "in vision," and also that the "Word was given to them by Jehovah" <note>original: "Jehovah"; the Hebrew name for God, used here to emphasize the Divine as the source of direct revelation</note>. When they were **in the spirit** or **in vision**, they were not conscious of their physical body, but were in their spirit; in this state they saw things that exist in heaven. But when the **Word was given to them**, they were then in the body and heard Jehovah speaking. These two states of the prophets must be carefully distinguished.

In the state of vision, the eyes of their spirit were opened and the eyes of their body were shut. In this state, they heard things spoken by angels, or by Jehovah through the angels; they also saw representations of things in heaven. In this state, they sometimes seemed to themselves to be carried away from one place to another, while the physical body remained in its own place. 

John was in this state when he wrote the Apocalypse <term>Apocalypse: from the Greek 'apokalypsis', meaning an 'unveiling' or 'revelation'</term>; as were Ezekiel, Zechariah, and Daniel at various times. It is then said that they were in **Vision** or in the **Spirit**. For Ezekiel says, *The spirit took me up, and brought me back into Chaldea to the captivity in the vision of God, in the spirit of God; thus the vision which I saw came upon me* (xi. 1, 24). He also says that *the spirit took him up, and he heard an earthquake behind him; and other things* (iii. 12, 24). Also, that *the spirit took him up between earth and heaven, and led him away to Jerusalem in the visions of God, and he saw abominations* (viii. 3, etc.). In the same way, he was in "the vision of God" or in "the spirit" when he saw the four animals, which were cherubs <note>cherubs: symbolic heavenly beings representing the Divine protection and the guard of the celestial heavens</note> (chapters i. and x.); as also when he saw...

<term>ultimates</term> <note>In this context, "ultimates" refers to the final, most external, or literal level of something spiritual. Here, it refers to the literal words of the Bible acting as the foundation for deeper meaning.</note>; as also in Isaiah (chapter 1:18): for wool is from sheep, by which the good of <term>charity</term> <note>In these writings, "charity" refers specifically to the spiritual love for one's neighbor and the desire to do good.</note> is signified; and snow is from water, by which the truths of faith are signified.

48. *And His eyes as a flame of fire*, signifies the Divine Wisdom of the Divine Love. By eyes in <term>the Word</term> <note>The author uses "the Word" as a title for the Sacred Scriptures or the Bible.</note> the understanding is meant, and thence by the sight of the eyes intelligence; and therefore in speaking of the Lord, the Divine Wisdom is meant. But by "a flame of fire" spiritual love, which is charity, is signified; and therefore, when said of the Lord, the Divine Love is meant. Hence then by His eyes being as a flame of fire, the Divine Wisdom of the Divine Love is signified. Swedenborg frequently critiques this creed for creating a distinction between Christ’s divinity and His humanity.</note>. When, therefore, His Divine is separated from His Human, by saying that His Human is not Divine, but like the human of another man, He is then "dead" among men. But concerning this separation, and the consequent "death" of the Lord in the hearts of the church, more may be seen in the *Doctrine of the New Jerusalem concerning the Lord* and in the *Angelic Wisdom concerning the Divine Providence* (n. 262, 263) <note>original: "Sapientia Angelica de Divina Providentia"; these are two of Swedenborg's primary theological treatises.</note>.

60. ***And, behold, I am alive for ever and ever***, signifies that He is eternal life. Since “I am He that is living” signifies that He alone is life, and that life is from Him alone (see above n. 58), it follows that “Behold, I am alive for ever and ever,” signifies that He alone is life to eternity, and that thus eternal life is from Him alone: for eternal life is in Him, and therefore from Him. “For ever and ever” signifies eternity. That life eternal is from the Lord alone, is evident from these passages following: Jesus said, *Every one that believeth in Me shall not perish, but shall have eternal life* (John 3:16). *He that believeth in the Son hath eternal life; but he that believeth not the Son shall not see life; but the wrath of God abideth upon him* (John 3:36; 6:40, 47, 48). *Verily I say unto you, he that believeth in Me, hath eternal life* (John 6:47). *I am the resurrection and the life; he that believeth in Me, though he die, shall live: every one that believeth in Me, shall not die to eternity* (John 11:25, 26: and elsewhere). Hence then the Lord is called “He that liveth for ever and ever” in the following places also in the Apocalypse: chap. 4:9, 10; 5:14, 10:6; Dan. 4:34.

61. ***Amen***, signifies the Divine confirmation that it is the truth. That “Amen” is the Truth, which is the Lord, may be seen above (n. 23) <note>The word "Amen" is derived from a Hebrew root meaning "truth" or "certainty."</note>.

That by having the keys of hell and of death is not meant the power of casting into hell, but the power of saving, is because it follows immediately after these words, *Behold, I am alive for ever and ever*, by which is signified that He alone is eternal life (n. 60); and the Lord in no wise casts any one into hell, but the man casts himself in. By keys is also signified the power of opening and shutting, in the Apocalypse (chap. iii. 7; ix. 1; xx. 1; also in Isaiah, chap. xxii. 21, 22; in Matthew, chap. xvi. 19; and in Luke xi. 52). The Lord’s power is not only over heaven, but also over hell; for hell is kept in order and connection by oppositions against heaven: and therefore, He who governs the one necessarily governs the other; otherwise man could not have been saved. To be saved is to be led out of hell.

->### THE APOCALYPSE REVEALED. [CHAP. I]<-

Heaven, concerning which something was said in the Preface. That the Church in the heavens, or the New Heaven, is meant by "the seven stars," is because it is said that "the seven stars are the angels of the seven churches;" and by an angel a heavenly society is signified. There appears in the spiritual world a heavenly expanse full of stars, just as in the natural world; and this appears so because of the angelic societies in heaven: each society there, to those who are below, shines like a star. From this, those in the spiritual world know the locations of the angelic societies. That "seven" does not literally signify the number seven, but rather everyone who belongs to the Church there—according to how each person receives the divine—can be seen above (n. 10, 14, 41). Thus, by "the angels of the seven churches" is meant the universal Church in the heavens, and therefore the New Heaven in its entire collective.

66. *And the seven candlesticks which thou sawest are the seven churches*, signifies the New Church on the earth, which is the <term>New Jerusalem</term> <note>In this theology, the "New Jerusalem" is not a literal city, but a new state of the Church and spiritual life on earth.</note> coming down from the Lord out of the New Heaven. That the candlesticks represent the church can be seen above (n. 43); and as "seven" signifies all (n. 10), the seven candlesticks do not refer to seven literal churches, but to the church in its whole complexity. In itself, the church is one, but it is diverse depending on how it is received. These varieties can be compared to the different jewels in a king's crown; they can also be compared to the various members and organs in a perfect body, which still function as one. The perfection of every form arises from various parts being suitably arranged in their proper order. It is for this reason that the universal New Church, with all its varieties, is described by "the seven churches" in the text that follows.

67. **THE FAITH OF THE NEW HEAVEN AND THE NEW CHURCH, IN ONE UNIVERSAL IDEA**, is this: That the Lord from eternity, who is <term>Jehovah</term> <note>The author uses "Jehovah" to refer to the essential Divine Being who took on human form.</note>, came into the world so that He might <term>subjugate the hells</term> <note>This refers to the act of bringing spiritual forces of evil and disorder under divine control.</note>, and <term>glorify His Human</term> <note>The process by which Jesus made His human nature divine, uniting it with the infinite Divine within Him.</note>;

It concludes by defining the core faith of this new era: that the eternal God became human to overcome evil and unite the human with the divine.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exposition of the opening chapter of Revelation, moving from the vision of the stars and candlesticks (the New Heaven and New Church) to the foundational principles, or "universals," of the faith that underpins this new spiritual era.</meta>

->### THE APOCALYPSE REVEALED. [CHAP. I]<-

...and that without this no mortal could be saved; and that they are saved who believe in Him.

It is said *in a universal idea*, because this is a universal of faith; and a <term>universal of faith</term> <note>In this context, a "universal" is a foundational truth that is so central it must be present in every single detail of a person's belief, acting as the structural base for everything else.</note> is what must be in each and every thing of it. It is a universal of faith, that God is one in person and in essence, in whom is a Trinity; and that the Lord is that God. It is a universal of faith, that no mortal could be saved unless the Lord came into the world. It is a universal of faith, that He came into the world that He might remove hell from man; and He removed it by combats against it, and by victories over it. In this manner He subjugated it, and reduced it to order, and under obedience to Himself. It is also a universal of faith, that He came into the world that He might glorify the <term>Human</term> <note>The "Human" (or *Humanum*) refers to the human nature—including the physical body and the natural mind—that God assumed through the birth of Jesus, which was then "glorified" or made Divine.</note> which He took upon Himself in the world; that is, might unite it to the Divine from which [all things are]. Hell being thus subjugated by Him, He keeps it in order and under obedience to Him for ever. Since neither of these things could be done except by temptations, even to the last of them, and the last was the <term>passion of the cross</term> <note>The suffering and crucifixion of Jesus, viewed here as the final spiritual trial in the process of overcoming the power of hell and uniting the human nature with the divine.</note>, therefore He endured that. These are the universals of faith concerning the Lord.

The universal of the Christian faith on man’s part is, that he should believe in the Lord; for through believing in Him there is conjunction with Him, by which is salvation. To believe in Him is to have confidence that He saves: and because no one can have confidence but he who lives well, therefore this also is meant by believing in Him.

These two universals of the Christian faith have been treated of particularly: the *First*, which regards the Lord, in the “Doctrine of the New Jerusalem concerning the Lord;” and the *Second*, which regards man, in the “Doctrine of the New Jerusalem concerning Charity, and concerning Faith,” and in the “Doctrine of Life for it;” and both now in the explanations of the Apocalypse.

<summary>This page defines the core "universals" of faith, focusing on the necessity of the Lord's incarnation to conquer hell and the requirement for humans to live well to truly believe and be saved.</summary>

### THE EXPLANATION.

69. In this chapter and the following the Seven Churches are treated of, by which are described all those in the Christian Church, who have religion, and from whom the New Church, which is called the New Jerusalem <note>The "New Jerusalem" refers to the holy city described in Revelation 21, interpreted here not as a literal city, but as a new spiritual era or a new state of the church on earth.</note>, can be formed; and it is formed from those who *approach the Lord alone, and at the same time repent of their evil works.* The rest, who do not approach the Lord alone, from the confirmed denial that His Human is Divine <term>Divine Human: A central doctrine in Swedenborg's theology, asserting that Jesus Christ's humanity was made fully one with His divinity, allowing God to be approachable and visible to mankind.</term>, and who do not repent of their evil works, are indeed in the church, but have not any thing of the church in them.

70. Since the Lord alone is acknowledged as the God of heaven and earth by those who are of His New Church in the heavens and those who will be of it on the earth—for that reason in the first chapter of the Apocalypse the Lord alone is treated of; and in these two following, it is He alone who speaks to the churches, and He alone who will give the happy things of eternal life. That it is He alone who speaks to the churches, is manifest from these passages: *Unto the angel of the church in Ephesus write: These things saith He that holdeth the seven stars in His right hand, that walketh in the midst of the seven golden candlesticks* (chap. ii. 1). *Unto the angel of the church in Smyrna write: These things saith the First and the Last* (ii. 8). *Unto the angel of the church which is in Pergamos write: These things saith He who hath the sharp two-edged sword* (ii. 12). *Unto the angel of the church in Thyatira* <note>These descriptions of the Speaker in each letter refer back to the visionary description of the Son of Man in Chapter 1, confirming that it is the Lord Himself addressing the churches.</note>
